title: 3-Read Friday #66: Motivation, Teacher PD, and Scripted Lessons
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #66 of 3-Read Friday opens with Dylan Kane's 'motivation fractal' -- a mental model where difficulty gradually increases within every unit of teaching time, from a single activity up to a full year, so students repeatedly rebuild momentum from an easier starting point. Jim Knight follows with five myths about teacher professional learning drawn from 25 years of research, including the claim that workshops change practice and that teachers who don't implement new strategies are simply 'resistant.' Holly Korbey closes by reporting on the growing adoption of scripted lessons in US schools, a trend Barton says has changed his own mind after years of opposing prescribed curricula. Barton frames the issue around three different flavors of structure -- structuring difficulty within lessons, structuring how professional learning actually changes practice, and structuring the curriculum itself via scripted lessons.
points: Kane's 'motivation fractal' claims the same difficulty-ramp pattern -- start easier than where the last unit ended, then gradually increase -- holds at every timescale, from a single activity to an entire year of school.

Knight's Myth 1 (workshops change practice) cites the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve directly: people forget 50% of what they hear within 24 hours, which is why standalone workshops rarely survive contact with the classroom without follow-up coaching.

Knight's Myth 2 reframes 'resistant teachers' as a misdiagnosis: people resist changes they don't find worthwhile or don't believe they can execute, not change itself -- meaning the fix is alignment, not persuasion.

Korbey's reporting captures a genuine shift in US practice and in Barton's own view: scripted lessons, once dismissed on principle, are increasingly defended on the evidence that systematic iteration of a shared script beats ad hoc individual lesson design in some departments.
quotes: I have long believed that the best way to motivate our students is not to make lesson content relevant to their lives or spice up presentations with fancy animations and GIFs but to make them feel successful.
Dylan explains this better than I could, complete with my favourite new motivational visual.
This article by Jim Knight challenged my beliefs on effective CPD and coaching.
There is plenty to think about here for teaching and learning leads and all teachers who engage in professional development.
As recently as 5 years ago, I was totally against scripted lessons. Hundreds of school visits later, I think the case for them in some departments is compelling.
